setting governable, pass an `AddConfig` proposal naming the key, its initial
value (which fixes the key's type for later updates), and the store: the epoch
config when every node must agree on the value for the whole epoch, the
instant config otherwise. A node reads an absent key as its built-in default,
so you can add the key before or after the node release that consumes it.

---

## Reconfiguration

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/reconfiguration.md

> How the Hashi committee transfers MPC key shares between epochs through DKG or key rotation as Sui validators change.

Reconfiguration is one of the most important parts of the Hashi protocol,
because it is the step where the old committee shares key shares of the MPC
key with the new committee (see [MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx)).

The Hashi service monitors the Sui epoch change and immediately starts Hashi
reconfiguration after Sui's epoch change completes. During reconfiguration,
Hashi pauses in-progress operations (for example, processing of withdrawals).
The new committee resumes and processes them after reconfiguration completes.

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Start Reconfig] --> B[DKG or Key Rotation] --> C[End Reconfig]
```

## How does a reconfiguration proceed?

On the happy path, a reconfiguration runs these steps in order:

1. A Hashi node detects a new Sui epoch while the Hashi epoch has not yet
   advanced to match.
2. Running nodes submit `hashi::reconfig::start_reconfig`; the first
   transaction to land forms the pending committee and sets the pending epoch
   change flag, which pauses deposit approval and confirmation, and withdrawal
   approval, commitment, and signing.
3. The new committee runs initial DKG (at genesis) or key rotation (in every
   later epoch), and each member ends with its `MpcOutput`.
4. Each member signs a `ReconfigCompletionMessage` with its BLS12-381 key, and
   nodes collect signatures until a quorum (2/3 of committee weight) produces
   an aggregate signature certificate.
5. On a key rotation only, nodes also collect the outgoing committee's
   signatures over a `CommitteeTransitionRequest`.
6. Within the same Sui epoch, a committee member submits `end_reconfig` (on a
   key rotation, together with `submit_committee_handoff` in the same
   transaction).
7. The chain verifies the certificate, advances the Hashi epoch, and clears
   the pending epoch change flag; deposits, and withdrawal approval and
   commitment, resume.
8. The new committee runs the presigning protocol; signing withdrawal inputs
   resumes once its presignatures are ready.

If Sui's epoch moves on before step 6 lands, [abort reconfig](#abort-reconfig)
resolves the pending reconfiguration instead.

## Start reconfig

Each Hashi node monitors Sui for epoch changes. When a new Sui epoch is
detected and the Hashi epoch has not yet advanced to match, the node knows
that it needs a reconfiguration. Every running node then submits
`hashi::reconfig::start_reconfig`, which is permissionless; the first
transaction to land forms the committee for Sui's current epoch:

```move
entry fun start_reconfig(
    self: &mut Hashi,
    sui_system: &SuiSystemState,
    ctx: &TxContext,
)
```

This sets a pending epoch change flag in the onchain state. Until
reconfiguration completes, the chain refuses deposit approval and
confirmation, and withdrawal approval, commitment, and signing
(`EReconfiguring`); users can still submit deposit and withdrawal requests,
which Hashi processes afterwards.
The active Sui validators that registered with Hashi and set their next-epoch
keys make up the new committee, leaving out any that
resigned or that governance ignored through an `IgnoreMember` proposal. Each
member's weight is its Sui voting power, and every threshold is a share of the
formed committee's total weight.

At genesis (the first Hashi epoch, when no MPC public key exists yet and the
committee must run initial DKG), the **launch switch**
additionally gates `start_reconfig`: it aborts until the publisher
has sent `hashi::finish_publish` (the `hashi launch` CLI command), which
finalizes the deploy configuration and hands the package `UpgradeCap` into
onchain custody. This gives the publisher explicit control over when (and
with which registered validators) the initial committee forms. After genesis
Hashi never consults the gate and applies no registration floor, because a
floor on a normal reconfig would let validators brick reconfiguration by
withholding registration.

## DKG or key rotation

The MPC key protocol runs among the new committee members. Which protocol
runs depends on whether this is the first Hashi epoch or a subsequent one:

- **Initial DKG**: if there is no existing MPC public key (the genesis epoch),
  the committee runs the distributed key generation protocol to produce a
  fresh master key.
- **Key rotation**: if an MPC public key already exists, the old committee
  redistributes its key shares to the new committee. The old committee
  members act as dealers and the new committee members act as receivers.

In both cases, each new member ends with an `MpcOutput`: its own key shares
and the MPC public key. See [MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx) for details.

Each committee member then signs a `ReconfigCompletionMessage` containing
the target epoch and the MPC public key using their BLS12-381 key. Nodes
collect signatures from each other through RPC until they reach a quorum (2/3 of
committee weight), producing a BLS aggregate signature certificate.
This ensures that a supermajority of the new committee agrees on the key
protocol output before the epoch transition finalizes onchain.

On a key rotation the outgoing committee must also approve the new one. Nodes
collect its signatures over a `CommitteeTransitionRequest` with the
`SignCommitteeTransition` RPC and submit that certificate through
`submit_committee_handoff`, in the same transaction as `end_reconfig`, which
does not activate a rotation without it. Initial DKG has no outgoing committee
and skips this step.

## End reconfig

A committee member submits the aggregate signature certificate onchain by
calling `hashi::reconfig::end_reconfig`:

```move
entry fun end_reconfig(
    self: &mut Hashi,
    mpc_public_key: vector<u8>,
    mpc_cert: CommitteeSignature,
    ctx: &TxContext,
)
```

The onchain contract verifies the certificate, commits the generated MPC
public key if DKG ran (or verifies that the key remains unchanged from the
previous epoch), advances the Hashi epoch, and clears the pending epoch
change flag.

Completion must land inside the Sui epoch in which the reconfiguration formed.
`start_reconfig` pins the pending committee to Sui's epoch, and both
`submit_committee_handoff` and `end_reconfig` abort with
`EReconfigWindowClosed` once Sui's epoch has moved past it; from then on only
[abort reconfig](#abort-reconfig) can resolve the pending state. Each
submission is bound to its target. `end_reconfig` reads it from the
completion certificate's signing epoch; `submit_committee_handoff` takes it
as an explicit `epoch` argument, because the outgoing committee signs the
handoff certificate and its signing epoch is the source epoch. The signed
handoff message already binds the target, so the argument adds no security;
it lets the chain name the failure. Both entries abort with
`EWrongReconfigEpoch` when a different epoch is pending (the target was
aborted and a replacement has formed), before it checks any signature. It reports a
submission whose own target already activated as
`EReconfigAlreadyCompleted` (another node's `end_reconfig` won the race, which
the node treats as success), whether or not the next reconfiguration is
already pending; nothing pending otherwise is `ENotReconfiguring` (the target
was aborted). The contract stores handoffs by source epoch, and a replacement can form
from the same source epoch after an abort. So for a handoff, the submission
counts as its own target only if the handoff stored under the certificate's
signing epoch (the source epoch) names the submitted `epoch`. Nodes
key their retry-or-give-up decision on which of these fires.

| Error | Raised by | Condition | What it means for the node |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `EReconfigWindowClosed` | `submit_committee_handoff`, `end_reconfig` | Sui's epoch has moved past the pending committee's epoch | Only [abort reconfig](#abort-reconfig) can resolve the pending state |
| `EWrongReconfigEpoch` | `submit_committee_handoff`, `end_reconfig` | A different epoch is pending (checked before any signature) | The target was aborted and a replacement has formed |
| `EReconfigAlreadyCompleted` | `submit_committee_handoff`, `end_reconfig` | The submission's own target already activated, whether or not the next reconfiguration is pending | Another node's `end_reconfig` won the race; the node treats this as success |
| `ENotReconfiguring` | `submit_committee_handoff`, `end_reconfig` | Nothing is pending and the target did not activate | The target was aborted |

After the new epoch begins, the new committee initializes the signing state
for the epoch by running the presigning protocol to generate a batch of
presignatures needed for the threshold Schnorr signing protocol (see
[MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx)). Deposits, and withdrawal approval and
commitment, resume as soon as `end_reconfig` lands; signing withdrawal inputs
waits until the new committee's presignatures are ready.

## Abort reconfig

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Start Reconfig] --> B[DKG or Key Rotation] --> C[Abort Reconfig]:::active
    C --> A
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

Reconfiguration can fail after `start_reconfig` has committed the pending
committee but before `end_reconfig` can safely advance the Hashi epoch.
Examples include:

- The pending committee cannot complete initial DKG because too much
  registered stake is offline or misconfigured.
- Key rotation cannot complete because the old committee cannot supply enough
  valid resharing material to the new committee.
- The new committee completes the MPC protocol but cannot gather a threshold
  BLS certificate over a single `ReconfigCompletionMessage`.
- The MPC output is inconsistent with the onchain invariant that the threshold
  public key remains unchanged across key-rotation epochs.
- Stale or incorrect validator metadata, such as invalid endpoint, TLS, BLS,
  or encryption key updates, formed a bad pending committee.

In these cases, anyone can call the `reconfig::abort_reconfig` entry function
directly, naming the pending epoch to abort. It is deliberately not a
governance proposal and takes no vote: the committees that could vote on one
are exactly the parties a stalled reconfiguration puts in doubt. The pending
committee might never finish DKG or key rotation, and the same offline stake
that stalled the reconfiguration can strand a proposal gated on the outgoing
committee's quorum. Instead the abort is bound to objective onchain
conditions, all checked in the same transaction:

1. A reconfiguration is in progress, that is, a pending epoch change exists, and
   the named epoch is the pending one (a stale transaction cannot tear down a
   different reconfiguration).
2. The pending epoch is not Sui's current epoch. `start_reconfig` pins the
   pending committee's epoch to Sui's epoch at formation time, so while the
   two still match the reconfiguration is inside its window and might
   legitimately complete. Only once Sui's epoch has moved past the target is
   the reconfiguration stuck by definition: [end reconfig](#end-reconfig)
   refuses to land after the window, so completion and abort are mutually
   exclusive by Sui epoch and can never race each other.

The launch switch is not re-checked: a pending genesis committee can only
exist because `start_reconfig` passed it, and the package `UpgradeCap` it
looks for never leaves onchain custody.

When these hold, the call clears the pending epoch change, removes the pending
committee (discarding any committee handoff certificate it had collected), and
emits `ReconfigAborted` with the aborted epoch. The current Hashi epoch,
committee, and MPC public key remain unchanged. After genesis, normal
operations resume under the last committed committee; at genesis there is no
committee yet, so Hashi returns to its pre-genesis state. Either way the Hashi
epoch now lags Sui's, and a fresh `start_reconfig` forms a replacement
committee from the then-current validator set.

Nodes drive this themselves. When a node sees a checkpoint from a later Sui
epoch while a reconfiguration is still pending, it stops working on that
reconfiguration, submits the abort (the chain settles the race between nodes),
and submits the replacement `start_reconfig` as soon as the abort is
reflected. A node that observes an abort it did not submit, including one an
operator sent by hand with `hashi committee abort-reconfig`, starts the
replacement in the same way, as does a node that comes up to find Hashi's
epoch behind Sui's with nothing pending, whether or not it can rebuild its
own signing state for the lagging epoch. The CLI commands are therefore
fallbacks for when no node is doing this: `abort-reconfig` refuses up front
when nothing is pending or the pending epoch is still Sui's current epoch,
and `hashi committee start-reconfig` submits the replacement, refusing when
a reconfiguration is pending or Hashi is already on Sui's current epoch.

Governance can hold the replacement off. While the
[`reconfig_hold`](config.mdx#reconfig_hold) config flag is set through an
`UpdateConfig` proposal, `start_reconfig` aborts on chain, so no committee
can form and the last committed committee keeps serving deposits and
withdrawals; nodes see the flag and do not submit. A reconfiguration already
pending continues, and so does `abort_reconfig`, so the sequence for staying
on the last committed committee is to set the flag and then let the nodes abort the overrun
reconfiguration. Clearing the flag does not itself start a
replacement: nodes submit `start_reconfig` on a Sui epoch change, on an abort,
and at startup, and none of those is a config change, so the replacement waits
for the next Sui epoch change unless an operator runs
`hashi committee start-reconfig`.

Every abort observed on chain, whoever submitted it, increments the node
metric `hashi_reconfig_aborted_total`. An abort means a reconfiguration
stalled for an entire Sui epoch with deposits and withdrawals halted, so it is
worth alerting on and investigating even though the system recovers on its
own.

## Which CLI commands can operators run?

Nodes normally submit these transactions themselves; `abort-reconfig` and
`start-reconfig` are fallbacks for when no node is doing so.

| Command | What it does | Refuses when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hashi launch` | Sends `hashi::finish_publish` at genesis, finalizing the deploy configuration and handing the package `UpgradeCap` into onchain custody, which opens the launch switch | None |
| `hashi committee abort-reconfig` | Submits the abort for the pending reconfiguration | Nothing is pending, or the pending epoch is still Sui's current epoch |
| `hashi committee start-reconfig` | Submits the replacement `start_reconfig` | Governance holds reconfiguration (`reconfig_hold` is set), a reconfiguration is already pending, a committee already exists for Sui's current epoch, Hashi is already on Sui's current epoch, or the fullnode's Sui epoch is behind Hashi's |

---

## Deposit

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/deposit.md

> How Hashi turns BTC sent to a deposit address into hBTC on Sui through the request, approve, confirm, and mint phases.

A deposit moves BTC from a user's Bitcoin wallet into the Hashi-managed UTXO
(unspent transaction output) pool, minting a corresponding amount of `hBTC`
into the user's account on Sui. The process has 4 phases:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Confirm] --> D[Mint]
```

The split between **Approve** and **Confirm** introduces a configurable
time-delay window (see
[`bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms`](config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms))
between the moment the committee certifies a deposit and the moment funds are
minted. This delay gives operators a chance to detect a faulty or fraudulent
approval and pause the service before the contract mints any `hBTC`.

## Request

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request]:::active --> B[Approve] --> C[Confirm] --> D[Mint]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

The user creates a Bitcoin transaction that sends BTC to a Hashi deposit
address. Each deposit address is a unique Taproot address derived from the
target destination address on Sui (see [Bitcoin Address Scheme](address-scheme.mdx)).
The deposit must meet the
[`bitcoin_deposit_minimum`](config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_minimum), which is never
below the dust minimum (`546 sats`), to avoid creating unspendable UTXOs on
Bitcoin.

After the Bitcoin transaction is broadcast, the user notifies Hashi by
constructing a `Utxo` and calling `hashi::deposit::deposit` on Sui.

You construct the `Utxo` from the Bitcoin transaction details:

```move
public fun utxo(
    utxo_id: UtxoId,
    amount: u64,
    derivation_path: Option<address>,
): Utxo

public fun utxo_id(
    txid: address,
    vout: u32,
): UtxoId
```

- `txid`: the 32-byte transaction hash in Bitcoin's internal byte order, the
  reverse of the hex txid that wallets and explorers show.
- `vout`: the output index within that transaction.
- `amount`: the deposit amount in satoshis.
- `derivation_path`: the Sui address used to derive the deposit address.

The user then submits it:

```move
entry fun deposit(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    utxo: Utxo,
    clock: &Clock,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

The function checks that the service is not paused (the contract accepts deposits
during a reconfiguration), that the deposit meets the minimum amount, and that
the UTXO is not already in the pool, active or spent. It then creates a
`DepositRequest` and places it in the deposit queue. Committee members start
monitoring Bitcoin for confirmation.

## Approve

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve]:::active --> C[Confirm] --> D[Mint]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

Committee members monitor the Bitcoin network for the deposit transaction. The
transaction must reach a sufficient number of block confirmations (see
[`bitcoin_confirmation_threshold`](config.mdx#bitcoin_confirmation_threshold))
before the committee considers it final. This guards against chain
reorganizations that could reverse a confirmed transaction. If the transaction
never reaches the threshold, for example because a reorg drops it, the
committee never approves the request. A request that the committee does not
confirm expires 24 hours after its creation, and the contract then deletes it;
the user can submit the UTXO again.

After confirmation, on Bitcoin Mainnet, each committee member with a TRM Labs
API key independently screens the deposit's Bitcoin transaction and Sui
recipient (see [Handling Sanctioned Addresses](sanctions.mdx)); other members
approve without screening. A member that rejects the deposit does not vote to
approve it.

After a node determines that a deposit request is both confirmed on Bitcoin
and passes its own screening checks, it communicates with the other members
of the Hashi committee and collects signatures from validators that agree to
approve the deposit. If a quorum of validators cannot agree to approve a
deposit, the node either retries the request later or ignores it
if invalid.

After the signatures reach a quorum, one validator submits the certificate onchain by
calling `hashi::deposit::approve_deposit`:

```move
entry fun approve_deposit(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    request_id: address,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

The function aborts while the service is paused or a reconfiguration is
pending, if the UTXO is already in the pool, or if the current committee has
already approved the request. Otherwise it verifies the committee certificate
against the current committee and records both the certificate and the
current clock timestamp on the request. The request remains in the deposit
queue, and the contract has not minted any `hBTC` yet.

## Confirm

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Confirm]:::active --> D[Mint]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

After approval, the deposit must wait through the configured time-delay
window (see
[`bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms`](config.mdx#bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms))
before anyone can confirm it. The window gives operators a chance to detect a
faulty or fraudulent approval and pause the service before the contract mints
funds. While the service is paused, the contract rejects both `approve_deposit`
and `confirm_deposit`, so pending approvals stay parked in the queue until the system is
unpaused, unless the request expires first. The 24-hour expiry described in
[Approve](#approve) counts from request creation, so it keeps running through
the time-delay window.

If the committee rotates before anyone confirms the deposit, the existing
approval becomes invalid and the new committee must re-approve the deposit,
which restarts the delay. The onchain `confirm_deposit` re-verifies
the stored certificate against the current committee, not the committee that
originally approved it.

After the delay has elapsed, any caller can call `hashi::deposit::confirm_deposit`:

```move
entry fun confirm_deposit(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    request_id: address,
    clock: &Clock,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

The function:

1. Aborts while the service is paused or a reconfiguration is pending, or if
   the UTXO is already in the pool (active or spent), before anything changes.
2. Re-verifies the stored committee certificate against the current committee.
3. Asserts that `approved_timestamp_ms + bitcoin_deposit_time_delay_ms <= now`.
4. Aborts if the request was never approved, the certificate no longer
   verifies, or the delay has not elapsed.

## Mint

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Confirm] --> D[Mint]:::active
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

After both checks in `confirm_deposit` pass, the function mints the
corresponding amount of `hBTC` and sends it to the Sui address in the UTXO's
`derivation_path` (a UTXO whose `derivation_path` is `None` mints nothing). The function adds the
deposited UTXO to the Hashi-managed UTXO pool, making it available
for future withdrawal coin selection.

---

## Withdraw

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/withdraw.md

> How Hashi turns hBTC on Sui back into native BTC through the request, approve, build, sign, and broadcast phases.

A withdrawal allows a user to redeem their `hBTC` on Sui for native BTC,
sent to a user-specified address on Bitcoin. The process has five phases:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]
```

## Who does what in a withdrawal?

1. **User**: calls `hashi::withdraw::request_withdrawal` with the `hBTC` and a
   Bitcoin destination address. Until the leader commits the request to a
   withdrawal transaction, the user can call
   `hashi::withdraw::cancel_withdrawal`, subject to a cooldown period.
2. **Committee**: approves the request with `hashi::withdraw::approve_request`.
   The leader then batches approved requests into a Bitcoin transaction and
   commits it with `hashi::withdraw::commit_withdrawal_tx`.
3. **Committee and Guardian**: the committee produces MPC signatures
   (`hashi::withdraw::commit_input_signatures`), the Guardian enclave produces
   the second signature, and the leader attaches it with
   `hashi::withdraw::finalize_withdrawal`.
4. **Leader and committee**: the leader broadcasts the signed transaction and,
   after the required confirmations, a committee member calls
   `hashi::withdraw::confirm_withdrawal`.

Beyond the request, the user's only optional actions are canceling and, if
the transaction gets stuck, fee bumping through child pays for parent (CPFP),
described in [Broadcast](#broadcast).

## How long does a withdrawal take?

The time from request to settlement depends mainly on these stages:

- **Batching**: the leader waits until a request has been waiting for roughly
  5 minutes since its submission, a threshold number of approved requests
  have accumulated, or the rate limiter can't fit the next request, whichever
  comes first. A request can wait longer if the Guardian's rate limiter is out
  of capacity, and Hashi never processes a request larger than the bucket's
  maximum capacity unless the limit increases (see [Build TX](#build-tx)).
- **One batch at a time**: the leader commits the next batch only after the
  previous one is fully signed.
- **Confirmations**: a committee member confirms the withdrawal after the
  transaction reaches
  the configured number of Bitcoin block confirmations
  ([`bitcoin_confirmation_threshold`](config.mdx#bitcoin_confirmation_threshold)).

## Request

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request]:::active --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

A user submits an onchain Sui transaction to request a withdrawal by calling
`hashi::withdraw::request_withdrawal`:

```move
entry fun request_withdrawal(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    clock: &Clock,
    btc: Balance<BTC>,
    bitcoin_address: vector<u8>,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

It is a private `entry` function, so you call it directly from a
programmable transaction block (PTB) rather than from other Move packages. A
PTB chains several commands in one transaction, and a later command can take
a value that an earlier one produced, so the `Balance<BTC>` can come from
earlier commands in the same PTB, such as `0x2::balance::redeem_funds` on the
sender's address balance.

- `btc`: the `hBTC` to withdraw, passed as a `Balance<BTC>`. Must be at least
  the [`bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum`](config.mdx#bitcoin_withdrawal_minimum).
- `bitcoin_address`: the destination witness program, either `P2WPKH` (20
  bytes) or `P2TR` (32 bytes). Hashi always pays a 32-byte program as `P2TR`.
  Because a `P2WSH` program is also 32 bytes, `P2WSH` destinations aren't
  supported.

The protocol enforces a minimum withdrawal amount to guarantee that every
request can produce a valid Bitcoin transaction even under worst-case fee
conditions. This minimum covers the worst-case miner fee (which pays for
both the user's transaction weight and opportunistic UTXO pool
consolidation) and the dust threshold for the user's output. See
[Fees](fees.mdx) for the full breakdown.

The contract stores the full `hBTC` amount with the request and places it in a
queue with a timestamp. The user can cancel their request at any point before
the leader commits it to a withdrawal transaction, including after approval,
subject to a cooldown period
([`withdrawal_cancellation_cooldown_ms`](config.mdx#withdrawal_cancellation_cooldown_ms)).
To cancel, the requester calls the private `entry` function
`hashi::withdraw::cancel_withdrawal`, which returns the refunded
`Balance<BTC>` for a later command in the same PTB, such as
`0x2::balance::send_funds` back to the sender.

## Approve

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve]:::active --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

On Bitcoin Mainnet, each committee member with a TRM Labs API key
independently screens the Bitcoin destination address and the requesting Sui
address (see [Handling Sanctioned Addresses](sanctions.mdx)); other members
approve without screening. A member that rejects the
request does not vote to approve it. If a quorum still approves, all members
must assist in completing the withdrawal.

Committee members communicate with each other to collect signatures to approve
the request. After the signatures reach a quorum, one member submits the certificate
onchain by calling `hashi::withdraw::approve_request`:

```move
entry fun approve_request(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    request_id: address,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
)
```

The function verifies the committee certificate and marks the request as
approved, so the leader can pick it up for transaction construction.

## Build TX

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX]:::active --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

The leader batches multiple approved requests into a single Bitcoin
transaction to amortize the fixed transaction overhead across users. The
leader waits for approved requests to buffer up before constructing a
transaction, until a request has been waiting for roughly 5 minutes since it
was submitted, a threshold number of approved requests have accumulated, or
the Guardian's token-bucket rate limiter (described below) can't fit the next
request, whichever comes first. This
balances latency for individual users against efficiency for the protocol.
The leader builds one batch at a time: it commits the next only after the
previous one is fully signed.

The leader takes approved requests oldest first and stops at the first one
that doesn't fit the current capacity of the Guardian's token-bucket rate
limiter, as tracked by the leader's own copy of it. That request and every
request behind it wait until capacity refills. The leader skips a request
larger than the bucket's maximum capacity every time, so Hashi never processes
it unless governance raises the limit; its owner can cancel it.

The leader then constructs an unsigned Bitcoin transaction:

1. **Coin selection**: select UTXOs from the pool to cover the total
   withdrawal amount (the user's withdrawn amount covers the miner fees).
   The coin selector might include extra inputs to opportunistically
   consolidate small UTXOs (see [Fees](fees.mdx)).
2. **Outputs**: one output per withdrawal request to each user's destination
   address, plus, when the inputs exceed the requested total, one change
   output back to a Hashi-controlled address.
3. **Fee calculation**: the leader estimates the miner fee through Bitcoin
   Core's `estimatesmartfee` RPC, floored at `3 sat/vB`, and deducts each
   user's share of the miner fee from their output. Validators independently verify
   that the fee is within acceptable bounds (at least `1 sat/vB`, at most 3x
   their own estimate).

The leader commits the resulting unsigned transaction and its txid onchain by
calling `hashi::withdraw::commit_withdrawal_tx`:

```move
entry fun commit_withdrawal_tx(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    request_ids: vector<address>,
    selected_utxos: vector<UtxoId>,
    outputs: vector<OutputUtxo>,
    txid: address,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
    r: &Random,
    ctx: &mut TxContext,
)
```

The function verifies the committee certificate, burns the `hBTC` from each
request, locks the selected UTXOs in the pool, adds the change outputs to the
pool as pending UTXOs, and creates a pending withdrawal record that all
validators can independently verify.

## Sign

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign]:::active --> E[Broadcast]
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

Signing is a two-step process matching the 2-of-2 Taproot script, which
requires both a committee (MPC) signature and a Guardian signature for each
input (see [Bitcoin Address Scheme](address-scheme.mdx)):

1. **MPC signature**: the committee runs the threshold Schnorr signing
   protocol (see [MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx)) to produce a signature for
   each input.
2. **Guardian signature**: once every input has an MPC signature, the leader
   sends the unsigned transaction and metadata, with a committee certificate,
   to the Guardian enclave, which checks the certificate and the request's
   timestamp, debits its rate limiter, and produces the second signature for
   each input.

The leader combines both signatures into the taproot script-path witness for
each input.

The leader commits the MPC signatures onchain in chunks, each under its own
committee certificate, by calling `hashi::withdraw::commit_input_signatures`:

```move
entry fun commit_input_signatures(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    withdrawal_id: address,
    indices: vector<u64>,
    signatures: vector<vector<u8>>,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
)
```

If a reconfiguration lands while a withdrawal is part-way through signing,
its still-unsigned inputs get fresh presignatures (see
[MPC Protocol](mpc-protocol.mdx)) from the new committee
(`hashi::withdraw::reallocate_presigs`); signatures already recorded stay.

The leader then attaches the Guardian signatures by calling
`hashi::withdraw::finalize_withdrawal`:

```move
entry fun finalize_withdrawal(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    withdrawal_id: address,
    guardian_signatures: vector<vector<u8>>,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
)
```

The function verifies a committee certificate over both signature sets and
marks the withdrawal fully signed. Each committee member re-checks the
withdrawal against its own copy of the rate limiter before signing that
certificate.

## Broadcast

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Request] --> B[Approve] --> C[Build TX] --> D[Sign] --> E[Broadcast]:::active
    classDef active fill:#298DFF,stroke:#1759C4,color:#FFFFFF
```

The fully signed transaction is broadcast to the Bitcoin network. The
committee monitors the transaction until it reaches the configured number of
block confirmations (see
[`bitcoin_confirmation_threshold`](config.mdx#bitcoin_confirmation_threshold)).
Once confirmed, a committee member calls
`hashi::withdraw::confirm_withdrawal`:

```move
entry fun confirm_withdrawal(
    hashi: &mut Hashi,
    withdrawal_id: address,
    cert: CommitteeSignature,
    clock: &Clock,
)
```

The function verifies the committee certificate, marks the withdrawal
confirmed and its input UTXOs spent, and promotes its change outputs from
pending to confirmed UTXOs. The withdrawal record stays in place until the
leader's garbage collection archives it with
`hashi::withdraw::archive_confirmed_withdrawals`, or, for a batch too large
for one transaction, `archive_withdrawal_requests` followed by
`finish_archive_withdrawal_txns`.

If a transaction gets stuck, CPFP handles fee bumping. Either the
withdrawal recipient spends their output with a high-fee child, or a later
withdrawal batch spends the stuck transaction's change UTXO and pays its fee
shortfall (see [Fees: stuck transactions](fees.mdx#stuck-transactions)).

---

## Hashi Node Backups

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/node-backup.md

> How node operators encrypt and restore essential node data with armored PGP backups, including YubiKey restore paths.

Hashi automatically backs up the data a node needs to rejoin the committee after
data loss. Every epoch, Hashi writes the node config, referenced key files,
and database snapshot to a tar archive, then compresses and encrypts it as an
ASCII-armored PGP message. The backup files use the suffix `.tar.asc`.
The key files and database snapshot can contain the node's operator, TLS, and
MPC private keys (see [Suspected node compromise](#suspected-node-compromise)),
so treat a decrypted backup as sensitive key material.

Encryption only needs the public PGP certificate, so the backup key does not
need to be present on the server during normal operation. Restore needs access
to the matching private key, either as a local PGP secret-key file or through
`gpg-agent` for YubiKey-backed keys. Because you can forward `gpg-agent` over
SSH, you can restore on a remote server using a YubiKey plugged into your laptop
instead of plugging the YubiKey into the server itself.

## Prerequisites

The section that uses each item describes it in detail:

- For a YubiKey backup key: a new [YubiKey 5 Series](https://www.yubico.com/products/yubikey-5-overview/)
  key with firmware 5.7 or newer, a USB-capable machine,
  [oct](https://codeberg.org/openpgp-card/openpgp-card-tools), [GnuPG](https://gnupg.org/),
  [YubiKey Manager](https://docs.yubico.com/software/yubikey/tools/ykman/), [jq](https://jqlang.org/),
  and a checkout of the [Hashi repository](https://github.com/MystenLabs/hashi).
- For a local backup key file: [sequoia-sq](https://gitlab.com/sequoia-pgp/sequoia-sq).
- For S3 backups: AWS credentials from the default credential chain, a node role
  restricted to `s3:PutObject` within its prefix, and recovery credentials with
  `s3:GetObject` (or `s3:GetObjectVersion` for a pinned version, plus
  `s3:ListBucketVersions` to inspect version history). See [Back up to S3](#back-up-to-s3)
  for the full Mainnet baseline.

## Create a backup key

### Option 1: Create a private key on a YubiKey (recommended)

We recommend generating a PGP private key entirely on one YubiKey and using its
public key to encrypt the node backup. This makes it practically impossible for
anyone to decrypt the backup without physical access to the YubiKey.

:::warning

Do not lose the YubiKey. Without it, you cannot decrypt backups encrypted to
its public key.

:::

Use a USB-capable machine and a new
[YubiKey 5 Series](https://www.yubico.com/products/yubikey-5-overview/) with
firmware **5.7 or newer**. Connect only this YubiKey; disconnect other smartcards.
Normal backups need only its public certificate, not a connected YubiKey.

1. Install [oct](https://codeberg.org/openpgp-card/openpgp-card-tools),
   [GnuPG](https://gnupg.org/) (`gpg` and `gpgconf`),
   [YubiKey Manager](https://docs.yubico.com/software/yubikey/tools/ykman/) (`ykman`),
   and [jq](https://jqlang.org/). Ensure your system's smartcard service is available.
2. From a checkout of the [Hashi repository](https://github.com/MystenLabs/hashi),
   run the setup script in an interactive terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/node-operator/provision-yubikey-backup.sh --output-dir ./backup-key
```

3. Follow the prompts for an optional User ID (Enter to omit),
   PIN changes, and physical touches.
   The script refuses cards that already contain keys, generates the private keys
   on-device, enables touch for decryption, exports public artifacts, and checks
   encryption and decryption. Keep the new User and Admin PINs in a secure password
   manager. Do not replace the factory attestation (ATT) key or certificate.
4. Save these **4 public files**. `<fingerprint>` is the full encryption subkey
   fingerprint:
   - `yubikey-backup-<fingerprint>.asc`
   - `yubikey-backup-<fingerprint>.attestation-device.pem`
   - `yubikey-backup-<fingerprint>.attestation-dec.pem`
   - `yubikey-backup-<fingerprint>.fingerprints.txt`

Use the `.asc` file directly as `backup-pgp-cert` in your node configuration.
The script also creates YubiKey attestation evidence. If desired, share all 4
public files to [assemble a multi-recipient backup certificate](#assemble-a-multi-recipient-backup-certificate),
which can verify the attestations.

For YubiKey restores with `--use-gpg-agent`, import the public certificate and
link the card in your normal GnuPG home (the script's test keyring is temporary):

```sh
gpg --import "./backup-key/yubikey-backup-<fingerprint>.asc"
gpg --card-status
```

Replace `<fingerprint>` with the generated filename's fingerprint and keep the
YubiKey connected; if using a separate recovery GnuPG home, use it for both commands.

Preserve the filenames. Store the YubiKey securely; do not share it or the PINs.
If setup fails, retain the public files and inspect the card before retrying.
You can restart provisioning if no data depends on any newly generated keys.
Otherwise, preserve the keys and follow the script's public-artifact recovery
guidance: wiping or regenerating them would destroy access to existing backups.

### Option 2: Create a local private key file

If you do not want to use a YubiKey, you can generate a PGP private key locally
and encrypt with it. Because a normal file holds the private key instead
of a YubiKey, there is a greater risk of unauthorized use of the private key.
Store the file carefully.

1. Install tools:
   - [sequoia-sq](https://gitlab.com/sequoia-pgp/sequoia-sq), Sequoia PGP.

2. Generate a new key pair. Be sure to update the name and email to real
values.

```sh
sq key generate \
  --own-key \
  --name "Your Name" \
  --email "you@example.com" \
  --expiration never \
  --without-password \
  --output private-key.asc \
  --rev-cert revocation-cert.asc
```

3. Export the public key to a file. Despite the name, this doesn't
   actually delete the private key, it just extracts the public key.

```sh
sq key delete \
  --cert-file private-key.asc \
  --output public-key.asc
```

4. Test encrypting a file to the public key:

```sh
echo "test message" > test.txt
sq encrypt \
  --for-file public-key.asc \
  --without-signature \
  --output test.txt.asc \
  test.txt
```

5. Test decrypting the file with the private key:

```sh
sq decrypt --recipient-file private-key.asc test.txt.asc
```

Confirm the output matches the original file contents, then delete the test
files.

6. Save the revocation, public key, and private key files in a secure location.

## Assemble a multi-recipient backup certificate

You can combine multiple YubiKey recipients into one OpenPGP certificate.
**Any selected recipient can independently decrypt the backup**; this is 1-of-n,
not threshold recovery. Participants exchange only public certificates, so the YubiKeys
never need to be in the same location. Hashi also supports software-key recipients.

This command requires the optional `backup-assemble-cert` feature. Build it with
`cargo build -p hashi --release --features backup-assemble-cert`; the binary is
`target/release/hashi`. Normal node builds omit this command and its GPG-agent dependencies.

The certifier's primary key must support certification and signing and be
available through `gpg-agent`. Pass its **public** certificate to `--primary-cert`:

```sh
hashi backup assemble-cert \
  --primary-cert certifier-public.asc \
  --recipient alice-public.asc \
  --recipient bob-public.asc \
  --output hashi-backup-cert.asc
```

Repeat `--recipient` for each public recipient certificate. If a certificate has
multiple usable encryption subkeys, select one with
`--recipient "alice-public.asc=FULL_ENCRYPTION_SUBKEY_FINGERPRINT"`.
The certifier is not automatically a recipient; list it explicitly if needed.
Use `--gpg-homedir PATH` to select a different GnuPG home. The output must not
already exist; configure it as `backup-pgp-cert` below.

The command reports each key's expiry. A finite certifier expiry limits the whole
certificate: replace it before then to avoid backup and node-startup failures.
If the certifier advertises SEIPDv2, every recipient must support it; a v1-only
certifier can include recipients that also support v2.

To verify a recipient's YubiKey provenance, add
`--recipient-attestation SUBKEY_FINGERPRINT DEVICE_PEM DEC_PEM`, supplying the
device attestation certificate and DEC statement. Repeat for each attested
recipient. Supplied evidence is always verified; add
`--require-recipient-attestation` to require it for every recipient.

For example, using the files exported during YubiKey setup (replace
`FULL_ENCRYPTION_SUBKEY_FINGERPRINT` with the `[E]` subkey fingerprint from the
recipient's `.fingerprints.txt` file, without spaces). Replace the recipient
paths with the matching files produced by the script:

```sh
hashi backup assemble-cert \
  --primary-cert certifier-public.asc \
  --recipient yubikey-backup-FULL_ENCRYPTION_SUBKEY_FINGERPRINT.asc \
  --recipient-attestation FULL_ENCRYPTION_SUBKEY_FINGERPRINT \
    yubikey-backup-FULL_ENCRYPTION_SUBKEY_FINGERPRINT.attestation-device.pem \
    yubikey-backup-FULL_ENCRYPTION_SUBKEY_FINGERPRINT.attestation-dec.pem \
  --require-recipient-attestation \
  --output hashi-backup-cert.asc
```

For multiple YubiKeys, collect each recipient's public certificate, device PEM,
DEC PEM, and `.fingerprints.txt` file under distinct filenames. Repeat both
`--recipient` and `--recipient-attestation` for each recipient. With
`--require-recipient-attestation`, software-generated keys cannot be recipients.

Verification checks the device certificate against pinned Yubico issuers and
checks that the DEC statement attests on-device generation of the selected key.
It does not establish current possession of the YubiKey or enforce a touch
policy, and it does not check X.509 expiry or revocation.

Before relying on the certificate, make a backup and confirm that each recipient
can restore that same archive independently.

Run `hashi backup test --backup-pgp-cert hashi-backup-cert.asc --use-gpg-agent`
for a temporary-message round trip with a YubiKey or GnuPG key, or replace
`--use-gpg-agent` with `--backup-pgp-secret-key private.asc` for a local private key.
Test files are automatically cleaned up on success or error.

## Configure Hashi backups

Every node config must provide `backup-pgp-cert` (a certificate file path or inline
armored text) and `backup-dir`:

```toml
backup-pgp-cert = "/path/to/hashi-backup-cert.asc"
backup-dir = "/var/lib/hashi/backups"
```

The `backup-pgp-cert` file is the public key you created in
[Create a backup key](#create-a-backup-key): the `yubikey-backup-<fingerprint>.asc`
file from Option 1, `public-key.asc` from Option 2, or a certificate from
[Assemble a multi-recipient backup certificate](#assemble-a-multi-recipient-backup-certificate). It is the public half of the backup key pair.
Restore uses the matching private half, passed as `--backup-pgp-secret-key`
(for example, `private-key.asc` from Option 2) or reached through
`--use-gpg-agent` for YubiKey-backed keys.

Use a persistent, node-specific backup directory outside the database directory,
with write access restricted to the node's user.

### Automatic cleanup

On epoch housekeeping, before the save, Hashi applies these rules in `backup-dir`:

1. Hashi deletes archives older than 14 days by filename timestamp, but keeps
   the newest current-epoch MPC recovery archive until it saves a newer one or
   that epoch ends. Ordinary backups cannot replace that recovery copy. Hashi
   keeps the newest archive of any kind while the node is still attempting
   saves, or up to 30 days otherwise. Archives that manual backups place in
   `backup-dir` follow the same policy.
2. Hashi removes abandoned `.hashi-backup-*` files and `.hashi-restore-*`
   directories older than 14 days by modification time, without retaining the
   newest staging entry.
3. Hashi leaves recent staging entries, symlinks, and unrelated files alone.
4. Entry errors do not stop the sweep, and a cleanup failure does not prevent
   the backup attempt.

Each sweep logs its epoch, directory, whether anyone requested a backup, and `removed`/`failed`
counts; expiring the newest archive also warns.

The node stages archives in `backup-dir`, then finalizes and syncs them to disk before
publication; it syncs the directory afterward on a best-effort basis. It logs a
directory sync failure at error level without failing the already-published backup. Failed saves
remove their temporary files and never overwrite existing archives.

### What operators must clean up

Automatic cleanup does not cover the following; handle them yourself:

- A powered-off node sweeps nothing, so delete a decommissioned host's archives
  yourself.
- Manual backups do not trigger cleanup. Apply [backup expiry](#backup-expiry)
  to all copies except the [monthly off-machine copies](#monthly-off-machine-copy).
- Restore staging and completed restore output contain decrypted keys and
  database data; use a private restore output directory. Automatic backup
  cleanup does not sweep completed restores, `.hashi-db-restore-*` staging
  directories beside the destination database, or restore output elsewhere.
  Remove these plaintext copies when you no longer need them.

### Backup expiry

Use a **14-day retention target**, measured from the archive's original creation,
for every backup copy except the [monthly off-machine copies](#monthly-off-machine-copy):
local archives (including the newest), other off-machine copies, and all versions of
the node's S3 uploads. Copying or re-uploading must not reset this target; the
[Back up to S3](#back-up-to-s3) section describes S3's versioning and deletion timing.

Active nodes check daily and refresh their current-epoch MPC recovery backup once
it is 3 days old, even during stalled reconfiguration. This intentionally preserves
recovery of the active shares; it does not extend retention for historical epochs.
If refresh is failing, preserve the last usable recovery copy and follow the
incident guidance below rather than deleting it to meet the target.

Old shares can still reconstruct the active MPC key after resharing. Keeping
backups indefinitely gives an attacker more time to collect enough decryptable
backups from the same epoch to recover that key. Expiry limits this opportunity
while preserving a recent disaster-recovery window. You keep the monthly off-machine copies
longer, for three months, so that you can recover the key even if an
attacker wipes every node.

Operators must configure deletion in each storage location, leaving out only the
[monthly copies](#monthly-off-machine-copy), which you destroy by hand under their
own rule; Hashi's newest-backup exception alone does not enforce this policy.
Account for Object Lock and monitor deletion failures or delays. Remove temporary
decrypted copies immediately after use.

During an incident, pause expiry for backups needed for recovery: disable the
applicable S3 lifecycle rules and other off-machine deletion jobs, and stop
destroying monthly copies. Hashi's local cleanup still runs, so preserve encrypted
copies outside `backup-dir` in a restricted location exempt from deletion. Confirm
the copies are accessible; changing lifecycle rules is not instantaneous. Resume
expiry and remove incident copies when recovery no longer needs them.

### Monthly off-machine copy

Once a month, copy the backup from the first epoch that starts in that month (UTC)
to storage that none of your nodes can reach, since anyone who takes over a node
can delete what it can reach. Do not put it in the S3 bucket that receives
automatic backups. Use that epoch's `-mpc-` archive, which holds the
node's [recovery record](#catastrophic-mpc-key-recovery). Recovery only combines
records from the same epoch, so every operator should copy the same epoch. Copy it
within 14 days, before local cleanup and S3 lifecycle rules remove it.

Test each copy when you make it, on a machine outside the validator fleet, by
exporting its recovery record with
[`hashi backup export-mpc-recovery-record`](#sharing-recovery-records) to your
`backup-pgp-cert`, then delete the export. If that epoch has no `-mpc-` archive or the

instead.

Keep each copy for three months after its epoch, then destroy it everywhere it is
stored, including old versions, replicas and snapshots. Destroy expired copies only
after this month's copy passes its test, unless your node has left the committee.
Keep a way to decrypt every copy you still hold, even after you replace
`backup-pgp-cert`.

## Restore from a backup

`hashi backup restore` decrypts an archive and extracts it into a directory you
choose. It installs nothing. The full procedure, from choosing a backup to
restarting the node, is in
[Backup and Restore](validators/backup-restore.mdx#restoring-a-node).
For S3 restore commands and an on-page recovery checklist, see
[Restore and infrastructure limits](#restore-and-infrastructure-limits) and
[Machine-loss recovery](#machine-loss-recovery) below.

## Back up to S3

Enable S3 uploads with this optional node-config table; both values are required.
Use a bucket name, not an S3 URI. Omit the table for local-only backups.

```toml
[backup-s3]
bucket = "my-hashi-backups"
region = "us-east-1"
```

Uploads and restores use the AWS default credential chain (environment, profiles,
or IAM roles), not credentials in the node config. The secure Mainnet baseline
requires operators to configure:

- A private bucket with S3 Versioning and [Object Lock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html)
  with **bucket-default retention**; Hashi does not set retention per object.
- A bucket policy explicitly denying object-creation `s3:PutObject` requests
  without `If-None-Match: *` (`s3:if-none-match`), rather than relying on the
  client's header alone.
- A node role restricted to `s3:PutObject` within its prefix, without object
  read or delete, bucket or retention administration, or governance-retention bypass.
  Restrict reads to approved recovery roles and keep their credentials off-node.
- CloudTrail **read and write object data events** scoped to the backup bucket,
  retained in an independent audit store outside backup writers' permissions.
  Use per-node credentials for attribution: events identify the credential
  principal, not a trusted archive creator.
- A **14-day remote retention target**, using [lifecycle expiration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-expire-general-considerations.html):
  - Expire current objects after **14 days** (`Expiration.Days: 14`).
  - Delete noncurrent versions after **1 day** (`NoncurrentVersionExpiration.NoncurrentDays: 1`),
    without retaining a minimum number of newer versions.
  - Remove expired delete markers with a separate rule
    (`Expiration.ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker: true`).
  Apply these rules to the backup prefix (or the whole dedicated backup bucket).
  Current expiry creates a delete marker; the data becomes noncurrent and is
  eligible for deletion 1 day later, not another 14 days later. Lifecycle uses S3
  upload time, so late uploads need separate expiry tracking. Object Lock can delay
  deletion, and lifecycle processing is asynchronous: this is not a hard deadline
  or a guaranteed recovery window.

Hashi neither provisions nor preflights these controls. Mysten Testnet's Pulumi
configuration defines the bucket and audit safeguards, but leaves read access
unchanged. Recovery-only reads remain Mainnet rollout work; node credential
provisioning is separate.

The node derives the destination from its identity, with no custom prefix:

```text
s3://<bucket>/<sui-chain-id>/<hashi-object-id>/<validator-address>/hashi-backup-epoch-<epoch>-<timestamp>.tar.asc
```

If the `-mpc-` marker is present after the epoch number, it identifies backups
containing MPC key-recovery information.

Scheduled backups upload the completed encrypted local archive once, without
retries or a queue. Failures preserve local backups and retention, and log the
local path and S3 URI.

### Manual backups

Stop the node before opening its database for a manual backup:

```bash
hashi backup save /path/to/validator.toml --output-dir /var/lib/hashi/backups
```

Replace `/path/to/validator.toml` with the path to your node config, and
`/var/lib/hashi/backups` with the directory to write the archive to (for
example, your configured `backup-dir`).

This saves locally, then uploads if configured. Add `--local-only` to skip S3.
Upload failure returns a nonzero exit status while preserving the local archive.
With S3 configured, a `--backup-pgp-cert` override with different usable encryption recipients requires `--local-only` or updating the configured certificate.

### Restore and infrastructure limits

Restore from a full S3 URI without the original node configuration:

```bash
hashi backup restore s3://my-bucket/<namespace>/hashi-backup-<timestamp>.tar.asc \
  --region us-east-1 --backup-pgp-secret-key /secure/secret-key.asc \
  --output-dir /private/restore
```

Here `<namespace>` is the `<sui-chain-id>/<hashi-object-id>/<validator-address>`
path from the destination template above, and `<timestamp>` is the timestamp in
the archive's filename. Take the full URI from the URI and version receipts you keep for each backup.

Use `--version-id '<version-id>'` to select an exact object version. Keys are
literal object keys, not URL-decoded paths. Recovery credentials need
`s3:GetObject` for the current object or `s3:GetObjectVersion` for a pinned version;
inspecting version history also requires `s3:ListBucketVersions`.

S3 restore accepts only encrypted `.tar.asc` archives. Choose
`--backup-pgp-secret-key` or `--use-gpg-agent` (with optional `--gpg-homedir`).
Local restores also accept plaintext `.tar` archives, which need neither decryptor.
`--region` is required for S3; it and `--version-id` are invalid for local restores.

Downloads use private temporary storage under `--output-dir`, and the command
removes them afterward. Restore publishes a complete extraction, refuses an existing
destination, and does not install files at their original paths.

Keep backup URI and version receipts, the region, and decryption-key access outside
the node. Use independently retained receipts and audit history to select an
exact version, then pin it with `--version-id`. Neither the newest object nor
successful decryption proves its origin: encryption does not authenticate the
creator. Unexpected versions or delete markers warrant investigation, but
lifecycle rules and authorized administrators can also create them.

### Machine-loss recovery

Use this path for accidental machine or disk loss without suspected compromise.
For suspected compromise, use the separate procedure below, not a snapshot restore.

1. Stop or fence the old node. Restore on a trusted replacement host into a
   private directory (`umask 077`); you need no original config or database.
2. Verify the restored chain, Hashi object, and validator identity against trusted
   records. Install the config and key files at trusted paths, not paths taken
   blindly from the manifest. Put `hashi-db-snapshot` at the configured `db` path;
   never merge it into an existing database.
3. Update config paths and endpoints, restrict permissions to the node user, and
   start the node. Check chain catch-up and committee participation.
4. Remove plaintext recovery output and temporary key copies when finished.
   Keep decryption-key access independent of the replacement host.

### Suspected node compromise

Assume the host-held operator, TLS, and MPC private keys have leaked. Even a known
pre-compromise snapshot can contain those same keys; its age does not make them
safe to restore.

For a **single compromised node with sufficient healthy peers**:

1. Fence the old host. From trusted infrastructure, use the validator account
   authority to revoke the old operator delegation and register fresh operator
   and TLS identities in onchain metadata. Follow the
   [key generation and registration](validators/keys.mdx#tls-key-dedicated)
   and [operator revocation](validators/keys.mdx#operator-key-day-to-day-signing)
   procedures with the replacement config; do not authorize recovery with the
   compromised operator key.
2. Provision a fresh machine with an **empty database**, not restored key material.
   Startup generates fresh node encryption and signing keys and registers them;
   see [server startup](validators/genesis.mdx#step-3-start-the-server).
3. Rejoin through [reconfiguration](validators/epoch-changes.mdx)
   with the healthy peers, and confirm the replacement identities and participation.

Suspected quorum-wide or global MPC key compromise requires coordinated incident
response, not this single-node procedure. Resharing preserves the global Bitcoin
key; it does not repair a stolen global private key.

## Catastrophic MPC key recovery

A zero-day compromise could steal and delete MPC key shares across the validator
fleet. Catastrophic data loss could also leave every node without its shares.
Backups allow you to recover the existing MPC key when no functioning committee
remains.

Scheduled backups with the `-mpc-` marker include `hashi-mpc-recovery.bcs`.
This file contains the node's shares and the information needed to combine them
with other nodes' backups to recover the MPC key. Recovery needs a sufficient set
of backups from the same epoch and works even after old onchain certificates are
gone. Manual backups do not include this file.

Operators should keep their [monthly off-machine copies](#monthly-off-machine-copy)
and keep access to their backup decryption keys separate from the validator fleet.
MPC key recovery is an incident-response operation, not part of ordinary node
restoration.

Recovery assembles the full MPC private key and writes it PGP-encrypted. You must
still handle it as a highly sensitive secret. Recovering it does not invalidate
a copy already stolen by an attacker.

### Sharing recovery records

For a coordinated recovery, use `hashi backup export-mpc-recovery-record` to
decrypt your backup locally and export only its recovery information, encrypted
to the coordinator's public PGP certificate. The command prints the recipient
certificate's fingerprint; verify it through a trusted channel before sharing
the export.

```bash
hashi backup export-mpc-recovery-record backup.tar.asc \
  --backup-pgp-secret-key /secure/operator-secret.asc \
  --output-pgp-cert coordinator.asc --output recovery-record.bcs.asc
```

Use `--use-gpg-agent` instead of `--backup-pgp-secret-key` for agent-backed keys.
Send only the encrypted `.bcs.asc` file; you need to share neither your backup decryption key nor
the full backup. The command never writes a plaintext record.
The coordinator can pass these files to `hashi backup recover-mpc-key` and decrypt
them with their own key.

---

## TypeScript SDK

Source: https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/ts-sdk.md

> TypeScript SDK for the Hashi protocol. Hashi is a decentralized Bitcoin collateralization primitive on Sui. Orchestrate native BTC directly from smart contracts—without centralized balance sheets.

TypeScript SDK for the [Hashi](https://github.com/MystenLabs/hashi) protocol. Hashi is a
decentralized Bitcoin collateralization primitive on Sui. Orchestrate native BTC directly from smart
contracts—without centralized balance sheets.

:::warning

**Not production-ready.** This SDK is pre-1.0 and under active development. The API may
change without notice and only Sui testnet and devnet are wired up. Do not use it in production
environments yet.

:::

End-user actions only: **deposit**, **request withdrawal**, **cancel withdrawal**.
Operator/committee/relayer calls are intentionally not part of this surface — those tools should
import the generated bindings under `src/contracts/hashi/` directly.

## Install

```bash
pnpm add @mysten/hashi @mysten/sui
```

`@mysten/sui` is a peer dependency.

## Setup

The SDK attaches to any Sui client via `$extend`. After extension, every Hashi method lives under
`client.hashi.*`.

```ts

const client = new SuiGrpcClient({
	network: 'testnet',
	baseUrl: 'https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443',
}).$extend(hashi());

const signer = Ed25519Keypair.fromSecretKey(/* … */);
```

> **Network support.** Sui **testnet** and **devnet** are wired up (Bitcoin **signet** by default).
> Prefer testnet — devnet support is temporary and will be deprecated. `hashi()` throws
> on any other network of the client it's extending. To target
> a custom or local deployment, pass `hashiObjectId`, `packageId`, and `bitcoinNetwork` explicitly.

> **Optional client options.** `hashi({ ... })` also accepts `btcRpcUrl` — a Bitcoin Core JSON-RPC
> URL, required for the [`client.hashi.bitcoin.*`](#bitcoin-rpc-optional) lookups — and
> `graphqlUrl`, which overrides the Sui GraphQL endpoint used by
> [`transactionHistory`](#transaction-history) (defaults to
> `https://graphql.{network}.sui.io/graphql`).

## Quickstart: Deposit BTC → mint hBTC

1. Derive the unique P2TR Bitcoin deposit address for your Sui address.
2. Send BTC to that address from any wallet.
3. Submit the funding `txid` + `vout` to Hashi for committee confirmation.

The committee watches the Bitcoin chain. Once the funding tx reaches `bitcoinConfirmationThreshold`
confirmations the committee **approves** the deposit; after an additional
`bitcoinDepositTimeDelayMs` safety window elapses the deposit becomes confirmable and `hBTC` is
minted to the `recipient` address. `view.depositStatus(digest).confirmableAtMs` reports that
earliest mint time.

```ts
const recipient = signer.toSuiAddress();

// 1. Get the deposit address.
const btcAddress = await client.hashi.generateDepositAddress({
	suiAddress: recipient,
});

// 2. Send BTC to `btcAddress` from any wallet, then collect the
//    funding tx's display-order txid and the vout that paid the
//    deposit address. (Display-order = the form mempool.space and
//    `bitcoin-cli` show — the SDK reverses internally.)

// 3. Record the deposit on Sui.
const result = await client.hashi.deposit({
	signer,
	txid: '0x<64-hex display-order txid>',
	utxos: [{ vout: 0, amountSats: 100_000n }],
	recipient,
});

if (result.$kind !== 'Transaction') {
	throw new Error(`deposit failed: ${JSON.stringify(result.FailedTransaction)}`);
}
// `hBTC` lands in `recipient`'s balance once the committee confirms.
```

A single funding tx may pay the deposit address on multiple outputs — pass them all in `utxos` and
they're batched into one atomic Sui PTB.

## Quickstart: Request withdrawal (burn hBTC → receive BTC)

Burns `amountSats` of `hBTC` from the signer's balance and enqueues a request for the committee to
send BTC to `bitcoinAddress`. The address is decoded client-side as bech32 (P2WPKH) or bech32m
(P2TR) and must match the client's configured Bitcoin network.

```ts
const result = await client.hashi.requestWithdrawal({
	signer,
	amountSats: 50_000n,
	bitcoinAddress: 'tb1q…', // P2WPKH on signet/testnet, or `tb1p…` for P2TR
});

if (result.$kind !== 'Transaction') {
	throw new Error(`request failed: ${JSON.stringify(result.FailedTransaction)}`);
}

// Pull the request id out of the WithdrawalRequested — needed if
// you later want to cancel.
const evt = result.Transaction.events?.find((e) =>
	e.eventType.endsWith('::withdrawal_queue::WithdrawalRequested'),
);
const requestId = (evt as { json?: { request_id?: string } } | undefined)?.json?.request_id;
```

## Quickstart: Cancel a pending withdrawal

Returns the locked `hBTC` to the signer. Only the original requester can cancel, only while the
request is still `Requested` or `Approved` (not after committee commitment), and only after
`withdrawalCancellationCooldownMs` has elapsed since the request. All three are enforced on-chain.

```ts
await client.hashi.cancelWithdrawal({ signer, requestId });
```

## Tracking a deposit or withdrawal

`deposit` and `requestWithdrawal` resolve to a transaction execution result whose
`Transaction.digest` identifies the submitted Sui tx. Pass that digest to the `view.*Status` readers
for a one-shot check, or to the `waitFor*` helpers to poll until a terminal state.

```ts
const digest = result.Transaction?.digest;

// One-shot status check — returns null if the digest has no Hashi event.
const deposit = await client.hashi.view.depositStatus(digest);
// deposit?.status: "pending" | "confirmed" | "expired" | "unknown"
// deposit?.approvalTimestampMs — when the committee approved (null until approved)
// deposit?.confirmableAtMs — earliest mint time = approval + bitcoinDepositTimeDelayMs
//                            (null until approved)

const withdrawal = await client.hashi.view.withdrawalStatus(digest);
// withdrawal?.status: "Requested" | "Approved" | "Processing"
//                     | "Signed" | "Confirmed" | "cancelled"
```

To block until the committee finishes, use the polling helpers. They resolve on a terminal state —
deposits on `confirmed`/`expired`, withdrawals on `Confirmed`/`cancelled`:

```ts
const info = await client.hashi.waitForDeposit(digest, {
	intervalMs: 15_000, // default
	signal: AbortSignal.timeout(600_000), // optional cancellation
});

const wInfo = await client.hashi.waitForWithdrawal(digest);
// wInfo.btcTxid is populated once the committee commits the Bitcoin tx.
```

## Checking hBTC balance

```ts
const { totalBalance, coinObjectCount } = await client.hashi.view.balance(signer.toSuiAddress());
// totalBalance — hBTC in satoshis; coinObjectCount — number of coin objects held.
```

## Transaction history

`view.transactionHistory` returns a unified, newest-first list of deposits and withdrawals for a Sui
address. Each item is a discriminated union — switch on `kind`:

```ts
const history = await client.hashi.view.transactionHistory(signer.toSuiAddress());

for (const item of history) {
	if (item.kind === 'deposit') {
		console.log(item.btcTxid, item.amountSats, item.approved);
	} else {
		console.log(item.requestId, item.btcAmountSats, item.status);
	}
}
```

Confirmed requests come from the on-chain index; in-flight deposits are discovered via the Sui
GraphQL endpoint (`graphqlUrl`). If GraphQL is unavailable the call still returns the confirmed set.

## Detecting already-used UTXOs

Before submitting a deposit, check whether its outputs were already recorded — re-submitting a
consumed UTXO aborts on-chain.

```ts
const results = await client.hashi.view.findUsedUtxos([
	{ txid: '0x<64-hex display-order txid>', vout: 0 },
]);
// results[0]: { utxoId, inActivePool, inSpentPool, isUsed }
```

## Estimating fees

```ts
// Withdrawal: worst-case BTC network fee + on-chain minimum. Pass a sender
// to also get a dry-run gas estimate.
const fees = await client.hashi.view.withdrawalFees(signer.toSuiAddress());
// { worstCaseNetworkFeeSats, withdrawalMinimumSats, gasEstimateMist }

// Deposit: dry-run gas estimate only.
const { gasEstimateMist } = await client.hashi.view.depositGasEstimate(signer.toSuiAddress());
```

Gas estimation is best-effort — a failed simulation yields `0n` rather than throwing.

## Reading governance state

Governance parameters — the pause flag, deposit/withdrawal minimums, confirmation threshold, deposit
time delay, and cancellation cooldown — are read through `client.hashi.view`, the same namespace as
the balance, status, history, and fee readers above. Prefer `view.all()` when you need 2+ values —
single round-trip, internally consistent snapshot.

```ts
const snap = await client.hashi.view.all();
// { paused, bitcoinDepositMinimum, bitcoinWithdrawalMinimum,
//   bitcoinConfirmationThreshold, bitcoinDepositTimeDelayMs,
//   withdrawalCancellationCooldownMs, worstCaseNetworkFee, ... }
```

## Errors

Direct methods throw typed errors before signing whenever a precondition can be checked client-side.
`instanceof` to distinguish:

| Error                        | Thrown when                                                                                                |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `InvalidParamsError`         | `txid`/`recipient` not 0x-prefixed 32-byte hex, or `utxos` empty/duplicate                                 |
| `InvalidBitcoinAddressError` | `bitcoinAddress` fails bech32(m) decode or HRP mismatches the BTC network                                  |
| `HashiPausedError`           | Governance has paused the operation (`deposit` or `withdraw`)                                              |
| `AmountBelowMinimumError`    | A UTXO or withdrawal amount is below the on-chain minimum                                                  |
| `HashiFetchError`            | The Hashi shared object can't be read or has an unexpected shape                                           |
| `HashiConfigError`           | A governance config entry is missing or malformed                                                          |
| `HashiGuardianError`         | The guardian `/info` can't be resolved, reached, or parsed, or the limiter isn't initialized (see `.code`) |

## Advanced: composable transactions

The direct methods (`deposit`, `requestWithdrawal`, `cancelWithdrawal`) sign and execute in one
call. For sponsored transactions, dry-runs, or bundling Hashi calls into a larger PTB, use the
`tx.*` builders — they return an unsigned `Transaction` and leave signing to the caller.

```ts
const tx = client.hashi.tx.deposit({ txid, utxos, recipient });
// …add more commands to `tx`, then sign and execute via your usual path.
```

Move-call thunks are also available under `client.hashi.call.*` for direct composition into
hand-built PTBs.

## Bitcoin RPC (optional)

When the client is constructed with a `btcRpcUrl`, the `client.hashi.bitcoin.*` namespace reads the
Bitcoin chain directly — useful for finding which output of a funding tx paid your deposit address,
and for checking confirmations before submitting a deposit.

```ts
const client = new SuiGrpcClient({
	network: 'testnet',
	baseUrl: 'https://fullnode.testnet.sui.io:443',
}).$extend(hashi({ btcRpcUrl: 'http://user:pass@127.0.0.1:8332' }));

// Which output(s) of the funding tx paid the deposit address?
const output = await client.hashi.bitcoin.lookupVout(btcTxid, btcAddress);
const outputs = await client.hashi.bitcoin.lookupAllVouts(btcTxid, btcAddress);
// each result: { vout, amountSats }

// Confirmation count — 0 while the tx is still in the mempool.
const confirmations = await client.hashi.bitcoin.confirmations(btcTxid);
```

Calling any `bitcoin.*` method without `btcRpcUrl` configured throws.

## Guardian rate limiter (optional)

Withdrawals are co-signed by the Hashi **guardian**, which throttles signing with a token-bucket
rate limiter. When the client can resolve a guardian URL — from `guardianUrl`, a custom
`guardianInfoProvider`, or the on-chain `guardian_url` config — the `client.hashi.guardian.*`
namespace reads the guardian's public, read-only `/info` endpoint to surface that limiter's
headroom.

```ts
// Guardian identity + limiter. `limiter` is null before the guardian is provisioned.
const info = await client.hashi.guardian.info();

// Projected capacity now, bucket fill %, and the refill-to-full ETA.
const status = await client.hashi.guardian.limiterStatus();
// { availableNowSats, bucketFillPercent, fullAtSecs, state, config }

// Can the guardian sign a 50,000-sat withdrawal right now?
const check = await client.hashi.guardian.canWithdraw(50_000n);
// { allowed, availableNowSats, estimatedWaitSecs }
```

`guardianUrl` overrides the on-chain `guardian_url`; a `guardianInfoProvider` overrides both (useful
for caching or a custom transport). The on-chain `guardian_url` is only published at launch, so a
client constructed beforehand re-reads the chain on each call until it resolves — throwing
`HashiGuardianError` (`code: "not-configured"`) meanwhile — then caches the URL once found.
`limiterStatus()` and `canWithdraw()` throw `HashiGuardianError` (`code: "not-initialized"`) before
the guardian is provisioned — use `guardian.info()`, whose `limiter` is `null`, to detect that state
without a try/catch.

## Bitcoin address derivation

Each Sui address maps to a unique P2TR Bitcoin deposit address with two script-path leaves: an
immediate 2-of-2 leaf `multi_a(2, guardian, derive(mpc_master, sui_address))`, and a delayed
MPC-only recovery leaf `and_v(v:older(delay), pk(derive(mpc_master, sui_address)))`. The MPC
child-key derivation replicates
`fastcrypto_tbls::threshold_schnorr::key_derivation::derive_verifying_key`; the guardian's BTC key
is read from the on-chain `guardian_btc_public_key` config, and `generateDepositAddress` throws
`HashiConfigError` until the deployment publishes it. See the
[Hashi address-scheme docs](https://mystenlabs.github.io/hashi/design/address-scheme.html) for the
full design.

---
